newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU prepares for annual battle over fish quotas.
newsitem.headline: EU prepares for annual battle over fish quotas.

text.p: European Union fisheries ministers are set for their annual battle over how much fish their fishermen can catch, trying to balance their economic needs against the need to protect scarce stocks.

EU officials said on Wednesday that although the European Commission has proposed little change in the catch quotas for most species, fierce in-fighting was still likely at the two-day meeting starting on Thursday.
"There are a number of contentious issues. It's likely to be a long night with a lot of horse trading," an Irish EU Presidency official predicted.
Ireland plans to start by talking to all the member states in turn to sort out their demands before formally attacking a 17-point agenda on Thursday afternoon.

Officials said one of the biggest battles will be over fishing in the Baltic for cod, herring, sprat and salmon now that Sweden and Finland's membership of the EU has ended their bilateral accords with Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
Germany, Denmark and Finland strongly oppose the proposed re-allocation of fishing rights.

Another potential flashpoint is over measures to halt the decline of sardine stocks off Spain and Portugal while Italy and Greece will be fighting hard over the introduction of quotas for bluefin tuna in the Mediterranean and Atlantic and for swordfish in the Atlantic.
The new quotas are based on recommendations by international scientists.

Because North Sea herring stocks have been so seriously depleted, the Commission wants to extend emergency measures introduced in July and fix a total allowable catch (TAC) for 1997 of 159,000 tonnes, roughly half the 1996 level.
It is also seeking for the first time to fix a quota for catches of herring by huge vessels hunting sprats for industrial processing into fish meal and oil.

The Commission also wants to slash North Sea sole catches by half to 12,000 tonnes because stocks are at critical levels. The reduction, which would also affect fishing for plaice, would affect mainly British and Dutch fishermen.

Among other issues, agreement may finally be reached on a satellite fishing vessel tracking system, officials said but they said there was little chance of agreeing a new multiannual fleet and fishing reduction programme.
